description: The first thematic cluster is the largest, comprising 29 articles (19.73% of the corpus), but with a low impact contribution (1.15 and 3.35 age adjusted average of citations per article in Scopus and Google Scholar, accordingly). This cluster focuses on ‘Disclosure Requirements’. A reporting entity discloses diverse financial information in its financial statements. Such disclosure is effective when it leads to a faithful and comprehensible representation of the entity, facilitating the comparability of financial information (IFRS Foundation, 2010/2018). Οne of the main issues that triggered the debate on the effectiveness of disclosures in financial statements was the perceived disclosure overload (IASB, 2012). AinE contributed to extending the discussion of this topic by supporting the Disclosure project of the IASB Disclosure Initiative through the work of Hellman et al. (2018). Their article is part of AinE’s special issue ‘IASB Research Forum 2017’. In this context, this cluster discusses issues related to disclosure quality, strategic disclosure, disclosure index, disclosure incentives, corporate governance, and earnings management. Earlier studies in this area focused on issues such as the disclosure of ‘pro forma’ earnings (Hitz, 2010), and the association between the voluntary disclosure of financial information and the amount of trade credit received (Ceustermans et al., 2017). More recently, studies have focused on investigating the disclosure practices by family firms (Vural, 2018), the voluntary firms’ disclosure choices related to enforcement reviews (Hitz & Schnack, 2019), and the association between segment disclosure quality and intensive board monitoring (KobbiFakhfakh et al., 2020). In addition, topics such as compliance with mandatory disclosure requirements in a particular jurisdiction for management reports (Vergoossen & Van Beest, 2021), the disclosure quality of alternative performance measures (Jana & McMeeking, 2021), and the association of risk disclosures and risk committee with banks’ performance (Nahar & Jahan, 2021), were discussed. Besides the main focus of the cluster, bibliographic coupling patterns also highlighted a minor corpus of literature related to earnings management. Indicative work in this subset sheds light on opportunistic factors in the capitalization of development costs (Brasch et al., 2022). The overall conclusion drawn from these studies underlines the relevance of disclosure and earnings quality in promoting transparency and trust. Since the majority of studies are limited to a specific country, future studies may provide a comparative perspective on the association between disclosure and earnings quality.

The second thematic cluster has 26 articles (17.69%), with a relatively high impact on Google Scholar (5.64) and a moderate influence on Scopus (1.66) indicating the cluster’s high impact beyond academia. This thematic area is predominantly dedicated to ‘Transition to IFRS’. The mandatory adoption of IFRS for listed companies in the EU marked a major regulatory shift in the history of accounting (Callao & Jarne, 2010). As of 1 January 2005, all EU listed companies are required to publish their consolidated accounts using IFRS (Delvaille et al., 2005). The aim of this project was to enhance comparability and transparency worldwide, with the ultimate goal of reducing the cost of capital (Hjelström & Schuster, 2011). In this regard, this cluster reveals views on implementation, adoption, convergence, and harmonization. Earlier studies in this area focused on investigating issues arising from the implementation of IFRS (e.g. Sucher & Jindrichovska, 2004), themes dealing with international financial reporting convergence (e.g. Delvaille et al., 2005), and topics analysing the effects of IFRS on either financial statements (e.g. Aisbitt, 2006) or management accounting practices (Colwyn Jones & Luther, 2005). As the research evolved, interest has shifted towards examining accounting methods within IAS 19 (employee benefits) after the mandatory IFRS adoption (Morais, 2008), the degree of harmonization and compliance in applying IFRS (Mechelli, 2009), and determinants of early transition (Fitó et al., 2012). These findings enhance our understanding of the challenges in adapting domestic accounting rules to the underlying principles of IFRS as well as of the approaches used by European countries to achieve the convergence. Future research could offer additional empirical evidence on the impact of new IFRSs, such as IFRS 17 ‘Insurance Contracts’, on the financial statements of European companies.

The third thematic cluster contains 19 (12.93%) articles, with a relatively high impact (1.82 and 4.72 on Scopus and Google Scholar, respectively), mostly focusing on the ‘Conceptual Framework’. The conceptual framework (CF) defines the objectives of financial reporting and comprises the fundamentals (underlying concepts) that help achieve these objectives (Johnson, 2004). From its definition it follows that this cluster reveals views on qualitative characteristics, reliability, and measurement uncertainty. In this context, AinE contributed to extending the discussion raised by IASB into the area of CF by publishing a separate special issue ‘The Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting’. Earlier studies in this area focused on topics related to the definitions of certain elements of financial statements, contributing to the IASB projects on the CF, (Barker, 2010; Nobes, 2012) and the value relevance of comprehensive income and other comprehensive income (Mechelli & Cimini, 2014). More recently, studies have focused on providing a better grasp of CF for financial reporting, including issues that arise in its construction (Dennis, 2018, 2019). In addition, the revised CF brought changes that generated research interest, including works that explore the impact of these changes on the IASB’s future standard-setting (Pelger, 2020) and the evolution of the meaning and role of the prudence principle from different perspectives (Alexander & Fasiello, 2021). The overall conclusion drawn from these studies is that there is a lack of empirical studies on the revised CF. Consequently, future studies can investigate the practical implications of the revised CF.

The fourth thematic cluster contains 16 (10.88%) fairly recent articles, with the second highest impact (2.13) on Scopus, mostly focusing on the ‘Non-financial Reporting’, a currently popular research trend to be found in AinE. The 2030 Agenda calls for companies to collaborate in achieving sustainability goals and guaranteeing a high level of transparency in financial markets. In that context, the Non-Financial Reporting Directive 2014/95/EU (NFRD), is viewed as a key measure in attaining these objectives (Cosma et al., 2022). This European law is the first regulatory endeavour to harmonize the Non-Financial Reporting (NFR) of large entities, mandating them to issue a non-financial statement with information on environmental, social, and human rights, anti-corruption, and bribery matters, as well as risk policies and performance (La Torre et al., 2020). These NFRD rules are revised and strengthened by Accounting in Europe 261 the introduction of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive 2022/2464/EU (CSRD), aiming, inter alia, to bring sustainability reporting on a par with financial reporting over time (European Parliament, 2022). Based on the contemporary reporting landscape, this cluster reveals views on sustainability assurance, sustainability reporting, CSR reporting, and NFRD. AinE contributed to extending the discussion about corporate reporting, publishing a special issue entitled ‘The Future of Corporate Reporting’. Earlier studies in this area focused on topics related to sustainability assurance practices (Gillet-Monjarret, 2015) and the association between voluntary environmental disclosure and the cost of equity (Déjean & Martinez, 2009). More recently, studies have focused on NFR harmonization (Aureli et al., 2019), the evolution of quantity and quality of non-financial disclosures from voluntary and mandatory perspective (Korca et al., 2021), and the impact of NFRD on the comparability of non-financial information (Breijer & Orij, 2022). In addition, a scoping review is provided on sustainability reporting in Europe (Dinh et al., 2023) and the executives’ position in the sustainability process (Klimczak et al., 2023). The overall conclusion drawn from these findings is that there is a lack of studies dealing with the effects of the CSRD. Consequently, future studies may shed light on the effect of the EU sustainability reporting standards.

The fifth thematic cluster contains 14 articles (9.52%), with a relatively low impact (1.42 and 3.79 on Scopus and Google Scholar, accordingly), mostly focusing on the ‘Regulatory Bodies’. In producing high quality accounting standards, the IASB follows a transparent process that considers input from diverse stakeholder groups worldwide (IFRS Foundation, 2016), the participation of which is a key element of the IASB’s legitimacy (Richardson & Eberlein, 2011). In this vein, the adoption of IFRS has led to the creation of regional accounting bodies such as EFRAG (Van Mourik & Walton, 2018). Against this backdrop, this cluster reveals views on legitimacy, standard setting-process, the IASB, and EFRAG. Earlier studies in this area focused on topics such as constituent participation of the International Financial Reporting Interpretations Committee (Larson, 2007), factors that influence participation in the IASB standard-setting process and ways to improve it (Orens et al., 2011), determinants of financial firms’ lobbying behaviour in the due process (Kosi & Reither, 2014), post-implementation review processes (Moldovan, 2014) and themes concerning the legitimation of the IASB (Crawford et al., 2016). More recently, studies have focused on providing qualitative evidence on the IASB’s standard setting from an internal perspective (Klein & Fülbier, 2019). In addition, insights into engaging in EFRAG’s consultation processes (Gäumann & Dobler, 2019) and understanding the US lobbying behaviour through comment letter writing are provided (Larson et al., 2022). The overall conclusion drawn from these studies is that efforts are made to enhance participation in the due process, both in terms of geographical diversity and through the inclusion of interest groups. These endeavours aim to significantly enhance the legitimacy of the IASB. Consequently, future studies can shed light on the constituent participation of the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) and investigate the factors influencing participation in its standard-setting process.

The sixth thematic cluster contains 13 articles (8.84%), with the highest impact (2.16 and 7.53 on Scopus and Google Scholar, respectively), mostly relating to ‘Audit Quality’. Audit quality is defined as the likelihood that the auditor will identify a misstatement in the client’s accounting system and report it (DeAngelo, 1981). This cluster reveals views on independence, audit fees, audit risk standards, non-audit services, and key audit matters. Earlier research in this body of literature focused on investigating the impact of different factors on auditor independence and audit quality such as mandatory audit firm rotation (Ewelt-Knauer et al., 2013), non-audit services and a cap on the volume of non-audit fees (Ratzinger-Sakel & Schönberger, 2015), long audit partner tenures (Garcia-Blandon & Argilés-Bosch, 2016), ethical culture in audit firms (Svanberg & Öhman, 2016), and joint audits (Haak et al., 2018). More recently, the research 262 M. Nerantzidis and S.E. Vatis interest has shifted towards examining topics of more contemporary concern, such as the effects of key audit matters (KAMs) on the communicative value of the auditor’s report (Köhler et al., 2020), the application of the reporting on KAMs in practice (Woudenberg et al., 2021), and the determinants of the total number of KAMs (Bepari et al., 2022). The impact of the Financial Reporting Council’s ratings on audit fees and audit firm switching (Yuan, 2021), issues related to audit quality in the public sector (Caruana & Kowalczyk, 2021), and some ideas for auditors to communicate more information about audit quality are also provided (Francis, 2023). Collectively, this stream of research indicates ongoing efforts to ameliorate audit quality with the goal of maintaining public trust. Future studies may explore how machine learning and artificial intelligence algorithms can contribute to this effort.

The seventh thematic cluster contains 13 articles (8.84%), with a relatively high impact both inside and outside academia (1.80 and 5.63 on Scopus and Google Scholar, respectively), mainly concerning ‘Endorsement of IFRS’. Endorsement is ‘an ongoing process by which individual new or amended Standards (including Interpretations) are formally approved for use in a jurisdiction’ (IASB, 2015, p. 14). Before they become binding for EU companies, IFRS and interpretations (IFRIC) are required to meet three sets of criteria, one of which is the true and fair view (Bischof & Daske, 2016). In view of this definition, this cluster discusses issues related to accounting language, translation, true and fair view, and legal certainty. Earlier research in this body of literature focused on investigating topics related to true and fair view (Wüstemann & Kierzek, 2006), legal certainty (Alexander, 2006), EU endorsement of IFRS and revenue recognition (Nobes, 2006). The evolution of this stream of research shows that interest has been moving towards examining the association between translation of IFRS and comparability which is one of the endorsement criteria (Dahlgren & Nilsson, 2012), investigating the impact of employing translated IFRS on decision-making (Holthoff et al., 2015), and analysing or translating accounting terms that can influence the effectiveness and efficiency of corporate communication (Nobes, 2021). Overall, the EU seeks to ensure that accounting rules comply with the requirement of legal certainty and maintain strict adherence to the IFRS endorsement criteria. It would be an interesting future prospect if the same applied to the endorsement process of the EU sustainability reporting standards.
